blocks.title: Bringing a batch into the EU
Sites, the API and the journey

summary.title: Why importing is different
points: A third country is any country outside the EU and EEA, such as India.
Extra steps: entry through an MIA site, full EU analysis of each batch, QP certification using it.
No agreement removes the testing step for India.
Indian sites need EU-recognised GMP; an Indian API needs a written confirmation.
Each step adds time and needs an owner: plan them from the start.

exercises.scenario: You compare two identical generics, one made in Germany and one in India.

questions.prompt: Which step applies only to the Indian one?
options: GMP compliance at the manufacturing site
Full analysis of each batch in the EU on import
QP certification, which German batches don't need before sale
questions.explanation: QP certification and GMP apply to both.

questions.prompt: Which document does an Indian API need?
options: A CEP issued by the Indian regulator for EU use

exercises.scenario: The project plan adds import steps only after the licence is granted.

questions.prompt: What's the risk?
options: They each take time and will push the launch
None; import steps only start once there's a licence anyway
questions.explanation: Build them in from the start.

questions.prompt: Is Switzerland a third country under EU law?
options: Yes, it's outside the EU and EEA
questions.explanation: Though it has an MRA with the EU.

summary.title: The EU importer
points: Third-country products enter through an EU site with an MIA: it receives, stores, tests and provides the QP.
Many MAHs contract an importer offering import, testing and QP release.
The batch release site is named in the dossier; changing it needs a variation.
Method transfer to the EU lab is often the longest step.
Choose the importer before filing; start method transfer early.

exercises.scenario: Filing is in two months and no importer has been chosen.

questions.prompt: Why is this urgent?
options: The importer is named in the dossier
The importer writes the clinical overview
It must be approved by the CMDh first

questions.prompt: Which importer task usually takes longest?
options: Customs registration at the border for the first shipment
Method transfer to the EU lab
questions.explanation: Late methods or reference standards slow it.

exercises.scenario: Two years after launch, the MAH wants to change to a cheaper importer.

questions.prompt: What's required?
options: A variation to change the batch release site
Nothing; it's a commercial choice outside the licence
questions.explanation: The site is named in the licence.

questions.prompt: What happens if the importer's lab isn't ready when the first batch arrives?
options: The batch is released on the Indian CoA
The agency tests it free of charge

summary.title: EU testing and the missing MRA
points: Each imported batch gets a full qualitative analysis, assay of every active, and all other licence tests in the EU.
MRAs (US, Japan, Canada, Switzerland…) let the EU waive re-testing.
India has no MRA with the EU, so every batch is re-analysed.
Needs an EU lab, transferred methods, reference standards and samples.
Days to weeks per batch, and a cost in the product's economics: book capacity early.

exercises.scenario: The same product is offered from a Japanese and an Indian site.

questions.prompt: Why could the Japanese batches skip EU re-testing?
options: Japanese sites are inspected by the EMA every year instead
The EU has an MRA with Japan

questions.prompt: What must the EU lab have before the first Indian batch?
options: A written confirmation for the finished product from the Indian regulator
Transferred methods, reference standards and samples
The restricted part of the ASMF

exercises.scenario: Finance asks why the Indian product's cost per pack is higher than expected.

questions.prompt: Which import step adds cost to every batch?
options: The written confirmation, which is charged per batch shipped
questions.explanation: It's part of the product's economics.

questions.prompt: How long does import testing usually take per batch?
questions.explanation: Add it to every batch's lead time.

summary.title: QP certification of imports
points: The QP's file is bigger for an imported batch.
CoA and batch-record review, EU import results, transport and temperature records.
GMP status of every site, API written confirmation and GMP declaration.
Deviations closed or assessed; compliance with the licence.
Missing paperwork delays more often than failed tests: agree a checklist before the first shipment.

exercises.scenario: EU test results are fine, but the shipment's temperature log is missing.

questions.prompt: Can the QP certify?
options: Yes, if the wholesaler signs for it
Not until transport conditions are documented and assessed
Yes, because the EU tests are what count for release
questions.explanation: Transport records are on the checklist.

questions.prompt: Where should the list of documents and deadlines be set?
options: In the licence and supply agreement's price schedule

exercises.scenario: A batch is held because the API's written confirmation expired last week.

questions.prompt: Was the QP right to hold it?
options: No: an expired confirmation can be renewed after release
No: it only matters when the API is shipped
Yes: it's part of the QP file and must be valid
questions.explanation: An expired confirmation is enough to stop certification.

questions.prompt: What's the most common cause of import delay?
options: Failed EU tests on the imported batch

summary.title: EU GMP status of Indian sites
points: EU authorities, usually the importer's supervisor, inspect third-country sites.
EudraGMDP lists authorisations, GMP certificates and non-compliance statements.
A non-compliance statement can restrict or stop EU supply, sometimes for every product.
Check site and address, scope, expiry, and any newer non-compliance statement.
Re-check before each major order; ask about history during the deal and keep a backup.

exercises.scenario: The tablet site's GMP certificate is valid, but covers only capsules.

questions.prompt: What's the issue?
options: None; any valid certificate covers every dosage form made
The scope doesn't cover your dosage form
The certificate must be from India
questions.explanation: Scope must match activity and form.

questions.prompt: Where do you check for a newer non-compliance statement?

exercises.scenario: Three months before launch, the API site gets a non-compliance statement.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for your launch?
options: Supply from that site may be restricted or stopped
Nothing, if your batch was made before the inspection
questions.explanation: It can stop supply for months.

questions.prompt: What would have reduced the risk?
options: Checking inspection history at the deal and keeping a backup source

summary.title: API written confirmation
points: Since the FMD, an imported API needs a written confirmation from the exporting authority.
It confirms GMP at least equivalent to the EU's, regular inspections, and notice of serious non-compliance.
Not needed for countries on the EU equivalence list; India isn't on it.
It covers a specific API and site, and expires.
Track expiry in the risk register and request renewals early.

exercises.scenario: The API's written confirmation expires next month; the next API delivery is in two months.

questions.prompt: What's the risk?
options: The API can't be imported, which blocks EU manufacturing
Only the finished product's CoA must be updated
None; the GMP certificate covers it

questions.prompt: What should already have happened?
options: A request to the EDQM to replace it with a CEP
A renewal request, tracked in the risk register

exercises.scenario: A partner asks why their US API needs no written confirmation but the Indian one does.

questions.prompt: What's the likely reason?
options: Written confirmations are only for finished products
US APIs are exempt from GMP rules
The US is on the EU's equivalence list; India isn't
The US API has a CEP, which replaces it

questions.prompt: Who issues the written confirmation for an Indian API?
options: The MAH, on the basis of its own audit of the site

summary.title: Logistics and customs
points: Products travel by sea (cheaper, weeks) or air (days); launch stock often flies.
Transport follows GDP, with data loggers for temperature.
A temperature excursion must be assessed by the QP before release.
Goods clear EU customs with the importer as consignee; CoA, packing list and records travel with them.
First launch shipments deserve extra buffer.

exercises.scenario: Launch is in five weeks and packs are ready in India.

questions.prompt: Which mode fits?
options: Sea freight, which is cheaper and fits within five weeks easily

questions.prompt: The logger shows four hours above the allowed range. What happens?
options: The wholesaler decides, as it receives the goods next
Nothing, if the EU tests pass
The QP assesses the excursion before release

exercises.scenario: This is the first shipment on a new route with a new forwarder.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson advise?
options: Extra buffer for new routes, paperwork and customs set-up
Ship by sea to save cost
No buffer, since GDP covers it

questions.prompt: Who is the consignee at EU customs?
options: The wholesaler in each launch country
questions.explanation: The MIA holder receives the goods.

summary.title: Typical delays and buffers
points: Most import delays come from a short list of causes.
Longest: a non-compliance statement or GMP problem at a key site.
Before every order: GMP status, written confirmation expiry, EU testing slot, document checklist.
After each shipment, log delays and causes.
Set buffers on your partners' real track record.

exercises.scenario: You're about to place the second commercial order with your Indian partner.

questions.prompt: Which routine do you run?
options: Only the price and quantity in the purchase order
GMP status, confirmation expiry, testing slot, document checklist

questions.prompt: Which risk usually causes the longest delay?
options: A non-compliance statement or GMP problem at a key site
questions.explanation: It can stop supply for months.

exercises.scenario: Your buffers are the same for every partner.

questions.prompt: What's a better approach?
options: Base them on each partner's logged track record
Remove buffers once the first launch is done
Let the importer set buffers based on its warehouse space
Use the largest buffer for everyone
questions.explanation: Note each delay and its cause.

questions.prompt: Why log delays after each shipment?
options: To report them to the agency

summary.title: Bringing a batch into the EU
points: Products from India need an MIA importer, full EU testing and QP certification.
The importer is named in the dossier; method transfer is often the slowest step.
No MRA with India, so every batch is re-analysed; MRAs exist with the US, Japan, Canada, Switzerland.
The QP file adds EU test results, transport records, site GMP and the API's written confirmation.
Paperwork, more than failed tests, causes delays.

exercises.scenario: You're filing in three months for a generic made in India.

questions.prompt: What must be decided before filing?
options: The EU importer and batch release site
The tender strategy for each country

questions.prompt: What should start right after the importer is chosen?
options: The first PSUR cycle for the new product
Method transfer to the EU lab

questions.prompt: List four documents the QP needs for an imported batch beyond the CoA.
questions.modelAnswer: EU import test results; transport and temperature records; GMP status of every site; the API written confirmation and GMP declaration (also batch-record review, deviation closure and licence compliance).

exercises.scenario: Your partner also offers the product from a Canadian site.

questions.prompt: What could change for EU batches from Canada?
options: No GMP inspection would ever apply
EU re-testing could be waived under the MRA

questions.prompt: What still applies to Canadian batches?
options: Nothing; they can go straight to wholesalers
Import through an MIA site and QP certification
A written confirmation for the finished product
questions.explanation: The MRA removes testing, not the front door.

summary.title: Sites, the API and the journey
points: Check each site in EudraGMDP: address, scope, expiry, any non-compliance statement.
A non-compliance statement can stop supply for months.
Indian APIs need a valid, site-specific written confirmation; track its expiry.
Air freight for launch stock; temperature excursions go to the QP.
Run a pre-order routine and log delays to set real buffers.

exercises.scenario: Before a launch order, you find: certificate valid, written confirmation expires in six weeks, EU lab slot not booked.

questions.prompt: Which two actions come first?
options: Chase the confirmation renewal and book the lab slot
Change the importer and file a variation
Switch to sea freight and add safety stock

questions.prompt: What else do you confirm?
options: The document checklist with the manufacturer
The PSMF and the QPPV's contact details

questions.prompt: Why should GMP status be checked before every major order, not just once?
questions.modelAnswer: A site can receive a non-compliance statement or let a certificate lapse at any time, and that can stop supply to the EU, sometimes for every product made there.

exercises.scenario: The first launch shipment arrives with a temperature excursion and no packing list.

questions.prompt: What happens next?
options: The QP assesses the excursion; documents must be completed
The batch is released, then investigated
The importer returns it to India automatically

questions.prompt: What would you change for the next shipment?
options: Confirm the document checklist and add buffer on this route
questions.explanation: New routes cause small delays that add up.

summary.title: Importing from India: the whole picture
points: Third-country products enter through an MIA importer named in the dossier.
No MRA with India: every batch is fully re-tested in the EU.
The QP certifies on a fuller file: EU tests, transport records, site GMP, API confirmation.
Sites need EU GMP status; a non-compliance statement can stop supply.
Indian APIs need a valid written confirmation; it expires.
Air freight, GDP, and a pre-order routine keep delays small.

exercises.scenario: You plan the first launch batch from India for 1 March.

questions.prompt: Which import steps add weeks after packing?
options: Shipping, EU import testing and QP certification
Only shipping, since EU testing is skipped for generics

questions.prompt: Which document, if expired, can block the API months before launch?
Which decision must be made before filing?
options: The importer and batch release site

exercises.scenario: Management asks why the Indian source has a longer lead time than an EU one.

questions.prompt: What's the main structural reason?
options: QP certification isn't needed for EU products
Indian sites can't be GMP-certified by EU authorities
No MRA with India, so every batch is re-tested in the EU
questions.explanation: Plus shipping and the extra QP file.

questions.prompt: What's the biggest single risk to an Indian supply chain?
options: Customs paperwork missing for the first shipment
A non-compliance statement at a key site
questions.explanation: It can stop supply for months.

questions.prompt: Summarise the pre-order routine in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: Before every order, check the GMP status of every site, the written confirmation expiry dates, the EU testing slot and the document checklist with the manufacturer.
